title: Statistical Analysis of Stop and Search Practices on Black Communities in the UK
text:
0.3 Key Findings

Raw national disparity: In 2024/25, Black individuals were stopped at 3.6 times the rate of White individuals, the headline figure shown on the accompanying dashboard. This is the unadjusted rate ratio (rounded to 1 d.p.), calculated directly from search counts divided by 2021 Census population denominators, with no covariates controlled.
Persistent and growing adjusted disparity: After controlling for region, sex, age, and reason for search, the adjusted incidence rate ratio (IRR) rises from 3× in 2020/21 to 3.3× by 2024/25,a statistically significant worsening. The adjusted figure is lower than the raw 3.6× because the model accounts for differences in regional composition and search type across ethnic groups; the gap between the two measures reflects those compositional differences, not measurement error.
Interaction effects: The compounding of ethnicity, search reason, and geography means that a Black individual stopped for drug-related reasons in London is searched at approximately 21.9 times the rate of a White individual stopped for non-drug reasons in the East Midlands, holding sex and age constant.
Regional anomaly: The South West has the highest Black/White disparity ratio (5.1×), exceeding London (3.6× pooled across all five years), suggesting nationally uneven patterns of disproportionality.
Outcome disparity: Black individuals have one of the highest arrest rates across all ethnic groups (16%, tied with Mixed), 2.7 percentage points above White individuals (13.3%), yet similar No Further Action rates (~69%), raising questions about differential suspicion thresholds.
Disparity cuts across all search reasons: The racial gap is not confined to drug stops. Every major reason for search, from weapons to articles for use in crime, shows a Black/White rate ratio substantially above parity, indicating a systemic rather than enforcement-specific pattern (see Section 5.10).
Missing ethnicity data is concentrated in a subset of forces: Self-defined ethnicity is voluntary: individuals are not required to state it during a stop, and around 1 in 10 records nationally has no ethnicity recorded. The rate varies substantially across forces, which limits the comparability of force-level disparity estimates (see Section 5.11).

These findings are intended to inform policy reform discussions and contribute to broader conversations on fairness and equity in law enforcement. An interactive dashboard accompanying this report is available at unjust.netlify.app.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
Stop and search is a key aspect of policing in the United Kingdom, involving efforts to identify and prevent criminal activity. Previous studies indicate that ethnic minorities, particularly Black individuals, are subject to stop and search procedures at higher rates compared to other groups (Home Office (GOV.UK), 2023; IER UK, 2023; Commission on Race and Ethnic Disparities, 2021; Vomfell and Stewart, 2021; Social Justice, 2020; Equality and Commission, 2010). The UNJUST project, initiated under the Statisticians for Society program (Royal Statistical Society (RSS), 2023), aims to provide a detailed, data-driven examination of these patterns to enhance understanding and inform policy discussions.
The project addresses four research questions identified by UNJUST:

Disproportionate Targeting: Do Black individuals in metropolitan areas experience higher rates of drug-related stop and searches compared to other ethnic groups?
Youth Impact: How do stop and search rates vary for young individuals (under 25 years old) in drug-related cases?
Trend over Time: Has the adjusted disparity in stop and search rates changed over the five-year period 2020/21–2024/25?
Outcome Disparity: Do post-search outcomes differ by ethnicity, suggesting differential thresholds for suspicion?

These questions align with broader concerns about systemic inequalities within policing practices and their potential impact on community trust and social justice.
To address these questions, the UNJUST project employs comprehensive data analysis and statistical modelling, utilising techniques that offer insights into the distribution of stop and search incidents across different ethnic groups. This report builds on the foundational work of researchers such as Vomfell and Stewart (2021), whose studies highlight the combined impact of officer discretion and the increased patrolling of ethnic minority areas. By analysing stop and search data from five complete financial years, 2020/21 to 2024/25, covering over 556,000 records, the project provides an updated perspective on the prevalence of these disparities and, crucially, whether they are improving or worsening over time.
One notable development in this area is the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) to support police operations. AI-driven tools, such as Live Facial Recognition (LFR), have been trialled by the Metropolitan Police in London to enhance stop and search methods. This technology enables real-time identification of individuals on police watchlists by scanning and recognising faces from distances of 10 to 20 metres. The system compares faces against databases containing thousands of known individuals, and when a match is detected, officers are alerted to potentially stop the individual for further questioning. According to recent reports, AI has the potential to improve the efficiency and objectivity of stop and search practices, contributing to more data-driven policing methods (Sylvester, 2024). While the UNJUST project does not incorporate AI-based stop and search data in its current analysis, understanding the role of emerging technologies is crucial for future efforts aimed at reducing disparities and enhancing the fairness of policing practices.
The findings presented in this report offer a rigorous, evidence-based analysis of the current state of stop and search practices, with a particular focus on racial disparities. By examining these issues through the lens of statistical rigour, the UNJUST project aims to contribute valuable insights to ongoing discussions about justice, equality, and effective law enforcement.

title: 3  Literature Review
text:
Stop and search practices by the police in the United Kingdom are intended to play a significant role in maintaining public order and safety. These powers, primarily governed by the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (PACE) (legislation.gov.uk, 1984) and the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 (CJPOA) (legislation.gov.uk, 1994), enable the police to intervene and prevent potential crimes, particularly in areas with higher levels of criminal activity. However, concerns have been raised regarding the disproportionate use of stop and search on Black and ethnic minority communities. This review synthesizes key findings from recent literature, exploring both the effectiveness of stop and search as a policing tool and the concerns over racial disparities.
Stop and search powers have evolved over time and have been utilized in crime prevention efforts. For instance, data from the Home Office for the year ending March 2023 indicates that 547,002 stop and searches were conducted in England and Wales, marking a 3% increase from the previous year. Of these searches, 14% resulted in arrests, highlighting their role in identifying potential offenders and intervening in criminal behaviour (Home Office (GOV.UK), 2023). However, disparities persist, as Black individuals were 5.5 times more likely to be stopped than White individuals in 2020/21, with this ratio decreasing to 4.8 in 2021/22 and 4.1 in 2022/23. These figures prompt further examination of the factors underlying such disparities (Home Office (GOV.UK), 2023).
Broader context on ethnic disparities across the criminal justice system is provided by the Ministry of Justice’s annual Statistics on Race and the Criminal Justice System (Ministry of Justice, 2023). The most recent edition documents persistent over-representation of Black individuals at every stage of the criminal justice pipeline: from stop and search and arrests through to prosecution, conviction, and custodial sentencing. Notably, Black individuals accounted for approximately 9% of arrests in England and Wales despite comprising around 3.5% of the population, a pattern of disproportionality that closely mirrors the disparities observed in stop and search data. This consistency across multiple points of contact with the criminal justice system reinforces the argument that the disparities measured in stop and search are not statistical artefacts of enforcement discretion alone, but form part of a broader, systemic pattern of unequal treatment (Ministry of Justice, 2023).
The causes of these disparities are multifaceted. Racial disparities in stop and search rates have been consistently observed, with several underlying factors potentially contributing to this trend. These include the demographic concentration of certain ethnic groups in areas with higher crime rates and operational strategies focused on specific high-risk areas. Localized crime trends, patterns of criminal activity occurring within specific geographic areas, often guide such strategies, with increased law enforcement activity targeting regions with higher reported rates of violent crime or drug-related offenses. Additionally, the subjective nature of suspicion during searches adds another layer of complexity. For example, the IER UK report on York highlights that Black individuals in North Yorkshire are 18 times more likely to be stopped than White individuals, partly attributed to over-policing in neighborhoods with higher crime rates (IER UK, 2023).
These observed disparities highlight not only operational challenges in stop and search but also raise critical questions about broader systemic inequalities that influence its application. Addressing these inequalities requires a deeper understanding of their socio-economic and historical roots, as explored in reports like the Runnymede Trust’s The Colour of Money (Runnymede, 2020) and the Equality and Human Rights Commission’s (EHRC) Stop and Think (Equality and Commission, 2010).
Stop and search is one of many tools used by the police to tackle crime, but its effectiveness and broader implications remain contested. The Runnymede Trust’s The Colour of Money report does not directly address policing tactics like stop and search but highlights the systemic racial inequalities that influence socio-economic outcomes and the lived experiences of Black and ethnic minority communities. These systemic factors, including discrimination and socio-economic disparities, may indirectly shape the context in which stop and search is applied and perceived. The report underscores that addressing such inequalities requires systemic changes, suggesting that targeted interventions in high-crime areas may not fully resolve underlying racial disparities without broader structural reforms to tackle economic and social inequities (Runnymede, 2020).
Similarly, the Equality and Human Rights Commission’s (EHRC) report, Stop and Think, critically examines the disproportionate use of stop and search powers (Equality and Commission, 2010). It highlights that while stop and search can provide a means to confirm or allay suspicion without arrest, the evidence suggests it has limited effectiveness in reducing crime rates, contributing only to a 0.2% reduction in disruptable crimes. The report also underscores that disproportionate targeting of Black and Asian individuals undermines trust in the police, negatively affecting community relations. The EHRC emphasizes that any effectiveness of stop and search should be balanced against these societal costs, suggesting that policing strategies must be both fair and proportionate to foster public confidence.
Concerns have been raised about the broader societal impacts of stop and search, particularly regarding its effect on community trust. Repeated law enforcement encounters can erode trust, fostering feelings of alienation and mistrust among minority communities. The use of facial recognition technology adds another layer of complexity (Sylvester, 2024), as advanced surveillance tools may reinforce perceptions of unfair targeting. While intended to enhance policing efficiency, facial recognition technology raises concerns about algorithmic biases that disproportionately misidentify individuals from minority groups, further compounding these perceptions. Such tools, when integrated into stop and search operations, may exacerbate perceptions of bias, particularly if algorithmic inaccuracies disproportionately affect minority groups. Nevertheless, the use of such technologies is arguably framed as a means to enhance data-driven decision-making and refine localized risk assessments to address specific crime trends.
Conversely, police forces emphasize that stop and search is used proportionately and in response to specific intelligence or local crime trends. According to the Commission on Race and Ethnic Disparities, operational decisions related to stop and search are often guided by crime data and localized risk assessments, which aim to address high-risk areas while maintaining fairness and transparency (Commission on Race and Ethnic Disparities, 2021).
The Centre for Social Justice’s Facing the Facts report (2020) highlights the importance of understanding socio-economic disparities both within and across ethnic groups. It challenges the broad use of the “BAME” (Black and Minority Ethnic) category, arguing that granular data, detailed and disaggregated information on individual ethnic subgroups, provides a more nuanced understanding of disparities in areas such as education, employment, and family stability (Social Justice, 2020). These disparities often overlap with patterns of localized crime, influencing both the prevalence of police interventions and public perceptions of fairness in policing practices. By addressing these socio-economic disparities and fostering inclusivity across public services, these strategies aim to reduce systemic drivers of racial disparities in policing and enhance community trust. Such interventions not only address root causes of crime but may also reduce the need for targeted policing strategies that disproportionately affect minority communities. In tandem with policing reforms, addressing broader socio-economic inequalities through targeted interventions in education and employment could reduce the systemic drivers of these disparities.
The Home Office’s report for 2023 indicates that 71% of stop and searches resulted in no further action, raising questions about the criteria for suspicion and the balance between proactive policing and the protection of civil liberties (Home Office (GOV.UK), 2023). The Home Office data underscores the scale of stop and search operations, yet the high proportion of no-action outcomes highlights the challenges of balancing proactive policing with civil liberties. While some may interpret this as a sign of inefficiency, it can also be seen as indicative of the difficulty in balancing public safety with the protection of civil liberties.
In response to these concerns, several recommendations have been proposed. The Commission on Race and Ethnic Disparities advocates for greater transparency and improved community relations, suggesting that community-led policing models and more rigorous oversight could help restore trust between police and minority communities (Commission on Race and Ethnic Disparities, 2021). Additionally, the IER UK’s anti-racism strategy for York emphasizes the importance of anti-racism training for public service professionals, including cultural awareness, unconscious bias, and inclusivity practices. The strategy focuses on fostering improved relations with York’s diverse communities by embedding anti-racism principles across all public services. It advocates for greater community engagement, encouraging active dialogue between public institutions and underrepresented groups to shape policies collaboratively. Furthermore, the strategy highlights the need for accountability through regular monitoring and transparent reporting on racial disparities, ensuring that systemic reforms lead to measurable progress (IER UK, 2023).
In conclusion, while stop and search remains a vital tool for maintaining public safety, evidence highlights its disproportionate impact on Black and ethnic minority communities, warranting careful consideration. These disparities stem from both operational and systemic challenges, including socio-economic inequalities, subjective enforcement criteria, shaped by an officer’s interpretation of ‘reasonable suspicion’, and broader societal impacts on community trust. Subjective enforcement, influenced by implicit biases and contextual judgments, exacerbates these disparities, perpetuating systemic inequalities. Achieving equitable and effective policing requires addressing not only operational practices but also the socio-economic and systemic factors that underpin racial disparities, ensuring a holistic approach to reform. Reform efforts must address these intersecting concerns to strike a balance between effective crime prevention and the protection of civil liberties. Future initiatives, such as the UNJUST project, will be instrumental in providing evidence-based insights to guide policy reforms, ensuring that stop and search practices are equitable, transparent, and conducive to public trust.

4.1 Data Sources
The analysis utilizes two primary data sources:
The analysis is inspired by Vomfell and Stewart (2021), who identified ethnic disparities in stop and search in the United Kingdom.
The selected variables, their code names, and data types are: number of stop and search events (number_of_searches, continuous), year (financial_year, categorical with five levels), region name (region, categorical with ten levels), ethnicity group defined by the person stopped (self_defined_ethnicity_group, categorical), sex (sex, categorical), age group (age_group, categorical), reason for search (reason_for_search, categorical), and population from census data (population, continuous).
Post-processing of the stop and search data includes: (1) verifying totals match published government figures ((GOV.UK), 2024); (2) filtering to Section 1 (PACE) and Section 60 (CJPOA) only; (3) converting categorical variables to factors; (4) removing vehicle searches (N/A - vehicle search), “Unknown” age group, “Not Stated” ethnicity, “Unknown” sex, and region 0 (British Transport Police, excluded because the 2021 Census provides no BTP-specific denominator); (5) converting age_group to a binary variable where 1 = under 25 and 0 = 25 or above; and (6) converting reason_for_search to a binary variable where 1 = Drugs and 0 = otherwise.

title: 4  Methodology
text:
GOV.UK Stop and Search Open Data (2020/21–2024/25): This dataset provides comprehensive records of stop and search incidents across England and Wales, including variables such as ethnicity, age, sex, region, and reason for search. The five-year extract covers the financial years ending March 2021 through March 2025, comprising over 556,000 records after cleaning. The data are released by the Home Office (Home Office (GOV.UK), 2024) and include all searches conducted under Section 1 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (PACE) and Section 60 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act (CJPOA).
ONS Census 2021: Used to obtain population denominators by ethnicity and region, serving as the offset in the rate models (National Statistics (ONS), 2022). We assume that the 2021 population counts remain a reasonable approximation across all five financial years, a limitation discussed in the Discussion chapter.

4.2 Data Cleaning Steps

Removal of Incomplete Cases: Excluded entries with missing or irrelevant data (e.g., vehicle searches).
Categorization: Transformed continuous variables into categorical factors where appropriate.
Legislative Filtering: Ensured that all stop and search incidents analyzed were conducted under Section 1 (PACE) or Section 60 (CJPOA).

title: 4  Methodology
text:
4.3 Data Processing and Filtering
The following steps describe how the raw data were processed and filtered prior to analysis. All operations are implemented in 01_load_and_clean.R and are fully reproducible from the raw files.

4.3.1 Stop and Search Data
The raw dataset is the Home Office stop and search open data tables (March 2021 to March 2025 release), distributed as a single ODS file covering five financial years (2020/21–2024/25). Processing proceeded as follows:

Vehicle searches removed. Rows where self_defined_ethnicity_group equals “N/A - vehicle search” were excluded because these records lack person-level demographics.
British Transport Police removed. Records coded as region 0 (British Transport Police) were excluded because the 2021 Census provides no BTP-specific population denominator, making rate calculations impossible.
Ethnicity harmonisation. The five Home Office ethnicity groups (Asian or Asian British, Black or Black British, Mixed, Other Ethnic Group, White) were retained and mapped to short labels (Asian, Black, Mixed, Other, White). Records where self_defined_ethnicity_group is “Not Stated” were set to NA and excluded from disparity calculations but retained for total-count comparisons and missing-data analyses.
Age binarisation. The original age groups (Under 10, 10–17, 18–24, 25–29, 30 or over) were collapsed into a binary variable: age_under25 = TRUE for Under 10, 10–17, and 18–24; FALSE for 25–29 and 30 or over. Records with “Unknown” age were set to NA.
Reason binarisation. reason_for_search was converted to a binary indicator: reason_drugs = TRUE if the reason is “Drugs”, FALSE otherwise. The original reason variable was retained for the reason-by-reason analyses in Section 5.10.
Region name standardisation. Two region names were recoded to match the ONS Census geography: “Eastern” → “East of England”; “Yorkshire and the Humber” → “Yorkshire and The Humber”.
Sex filtering. Records with sex recorded as “Unknown” were excluded. Only “Male” and “Female” were retained.
Legislative scope. The raw data include searches under Section 1 (PACE) and Section 60 (CJPOA) only, as released by the Home Office. No additional legislative filtering was required.



4.3.2 Census Data
Population denominators were drawn from the ONS 2021 Census table on population by ethnicity and region (National Statistics (ONS), 2022). Processing steps:

Ethnicity type filtered. Only rows with ethnicity_type = "ONS 2021 5+1" (the five main groups plus Other) were retained.
National aggregate excluded. The “All - England And Wales” geography row was removed; only regional totals were kept.
Five ethnic groups retained. Asian, Black, White, Mixed, and Other,matching the stop and search categories.



4.3.3 Merging and Aggregation
Stop and search records were aggregated by financial year, region, and ethnicity (after excluding rows with missing ethnicity), then joined to the census population by region and ethnicity. This produced a merged dataset of stratified counts with population denominators, from which per-1,000 rates and model offsets were calculated.
For the Poisson regression models, the data were further stratified by sex, age group (binary), and reason for search (binary), producing the full factorial modelling dataset.


4.3.4 Additional Filtering in Derived Analyses

Reason-by-reason disparity (Section 5.10): Black/White rate ratios were computed per search reason. Reasons with fewer than 1,000 total searches across all years and ethnicities were excluded as unreliable.
Missing ethnicity analysis (Section 5.11): Force-level missingness was computed from the full dataset (including NA ethnicity records). Only forces with data in at least three of the five years were included in the persistent-missingness ranking.
NFA and outcome analysis: Computed from all records with non-missing ethnicity, without further exclusions.



4.3.5 Reproducibility
All scripts are available in the project repository (analysis/01_load_and_clean.R through analysis/06_export_for_dashboard.R). Raw data can be downloaded via data/download_data.sh, which retrieves the Home Office ODS file and ONS census CSV from their published URLs. Running the scripts in numerical order from the repository root will reproduce all processed datasets and analysis outputs.

title: 4  Methodology
text:
4.4 The Pooled Model
We model total searches as the dependent variable (\(Y\)) with region, ethnic group, sex, age group, and reason for search as independent variables. Because the raw count data exhibited severe overdispersion (estimated dispersion parameter \(\hat{\phi} = 181.8\); see Section 4.5), we use a Quasi-Poisson generalised linear model with a log link and the stratified census population as an offset.
Let \(Y\) be the number of searches observed for population stratum \(N\). The mean is \(\mu = N \exp(\mathbf{X}^T \beta)\), with linear predictor \(\eta = \mathbf{X}^T \beta + \log N\). For the \(i\)-th stratum:
\[\mu_i = n_i \exp\!\bigl(x_i^T \beta\bigr) = \exp\!\bigl(x_i^T \beta + \log n_i\bigr) \tag{1}\]
using the notation in Davison (2009). Expanding the linear predictor over the five-year period:
\[\begin{align*}
\log(\mu_i) &= \log(pop_i) + \beta_0 + \sum_{h=2}^{5} \beta_{1h} I(\text{year}_{ih}) + \sum_{l=1}^{L} \beta_{3l} I(\text{region}_{il}) + \sum_{j=1}^{J} \beta_{4j} I(\text{ethnic}_{ij}) \\
&\quad + \beta_5 I(\text{sex}_{i,\text{Male}}) + \beta_7 I(\text{age}_{i,<25}) + \beta_8 I(\text{drugs}_{i1}) \tag{2}
\end{align*}\]
where \(I(\cdot)\) is an indicator variable. Reference levels are: financial year 2020/21, region East Midlands, ethnicity White, sex Female, age group 25 and above, and reason non-drug-related.
Variable descriptions:

\(pop_i\): census population count for stratum \(i\) (National Statistics (ONS), 2022)
\(I(\text{year}_{ih})\) (financial_year): five levels: 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25
\(I(\text{region}_{il})\) (region): ten regions in England and Wales (East Midlands as reference)
\(I(\text{ethnic}_{ij})\) (self_defined_ethnicity_group): five groups: Asian or Asian British, Black or Black British, Mixed, Other Ethnic Group, White (reference)
\(I(\text{sex}_{i,\text{Male}})\) (sex): Male vs Female (reference)
\(I(\text{age}_{i,<25})\) (age_group): binary: 1 if under 25, 0 otherwise
\(I(\text{drugs}_{i1})\) (reason_for_search): binary: 1 if drug-related, 0 otherwise

title: 4  Methodology
text:
4.5 Quasi-Poisson: Justification
A standard Poisson model assumes that the mean equals the variance (\(\text{Var}(Y) = \mu\)). In practice, count data on policing activity routinely exhibit overdispersion, variance substantially exceeding the mean, due to unmodelled heterogeneity across police forces, local crime environments, and seasonal patterns.
Fitting the pooled model with a standard Poisson family yields a residual deviance of 342,749 on 1,950 degrees of freedom, producing an estimated dispersion parameter of:
\[\hat{\phi} = \frac{\text{Residual deviance}}{\text{df}} = \frac{342{,}749}{1{,}950} \approx 181.8\]
This is far greater than 1, confirming severe overdispersion. A Quasi-Poisson model retains the same coefficient estimates as Poisson but scales all standard errors by \(\sqrt{\hat{\phi}}\), producing correct (wider) confidence intervals and conservative inference. Using a Poisson family without this correction would dramatically understate uncertainty and inflate the apparent precision of the IRR estimates.
Note that Quasi-Poisson models do not yield a finite AIC; model adequacy is instead assessed via the pseudo-R² (Cohen, 1988) and residual deviance diagnostics.

title: 4  Methodology
text:
4.6 Per-Year IRR Models
To examine whether the adjusted disparity in stop and search rates has changed over time (Research Question 3), we fit five separate Quasi-Poisson models, one per financial year, each using the same specification as the pooled model but without the financial_year term. This yields year-specific incidence rate ratios (IRRs) and 95% confidence intervals for each ethnic group relative to White individuals. The per-year Black IRRs are presented in the Results chapter (Section 5.6).

title: 4  Methodology
section: 4.7 Random Forest Model as a Complementary Analysis
text:
4.7 Random Forest Model as a Complementary Analysis

4.7.1 Rationale for Using Random Forest in Addition to the Main Model
The main model for this analysis employs a regression approach to examine the impact of various demographic and contextual factors on stop-and-search practices. While regression models are powerful for estimating specific associations and providing clear interpretations through coefficients, they have some limitations. Specifically, regression models assume linearity and often require predefined interactions between predictors to fully capture complex relationships within the data. In contrast, random forests are a non-parametric machine learning approach that can automatically capture both non-linear relationships and interactions among variables without needing explicit specification. This capability makes random forests an ideal complementary tool for exploring complex, multi-dimensional patterns within stop-and-search data.
Using random forests in addition to the main model serves several key purposes:

Validation and Robustness: The random forest model validates findings from the regression model by identifying the most influential predictors of stop-and-search activity without assuming specific linear relationships. If similar predictors emerge as significant in both models, this strengthens the evidence for their role in influencing stop-and-search practices.
Non-linear and Interaction Effects: Random forests are effective at capturing non-linear relationships and variable interactions, allowing for deeper insights into how combinations of factors (e.g., ethnicity and region) may contribute to disparities in stop-and-search practices. This is particularly relevant for understanding complex social phenomena where the effects of variables are unlikely to be purely linear or independent.
Variable Importance: Unlike regression coefficients, which quantify the effect of each predictor, random forests provide variable importance scores. These scores allow us to rank predictors by their influence on the outcome (total stop-and-search counts), offering an alternative perspective on which factors most drive stop-and-search activity.

By using random forests alongside the main regression model, we obtain a comprehensive view of stop-and-search patterns, combining the interpretability of regression with the flexibility and interaction-capturing ability of random forests.


4.7.2 Overview of the Random Forest Model
The random forest model applied in this study is designed to predict total stop-and-search counts using demographic, geographic, and contextual variables. Random forests operate by constructing an ensemble of decision trees, each built from a bootstrap sample of the original data. Each tree independently predicts the outcome, and the final prediction for each observation is obtained by aggregating the predictions across all trees (for regression, this is typically the mean prediction). Key steps and features of the random forest model are as follows:

Bootstrap Sampling and Tree Construction:

For each decision tree in the forest, a random sample (with replacement) is drawn from the dataset, which is known as bootstrap sampling. This approach introduces variation among the trees, enhancing the model’s robustness and reducing overfitting to any one sample.
At each node of a tree, a random subset of predictors is selected as candidate variables for splitting. This process, known as feature bagging, ensures that each tree explores different predictor combinations, further improving the model’s generalization to new data.

Split Criteria and Aggregation:

The model uses mean squared error (MSE) as the criterion for creating splits in each tree, which minimizes the variance within each split group. This criterion is effective for identifying variable thresholds associated with differences in stop-and-search counts.
Once all trees are built, the model aggregates predictions from each tree to produce a single, overall prediction for each observation. This aggregation (averaging) process improves accuracy and stability, as it reduces the likelihood of overfitting that may occur in individual decision trees.

Variable Importance Measures:

The random forest model provides variable importance scores, specifically % Increase in Mean Squared Error (%IncMSE), which indicates the decrease in prediction accuracy when a variable is removed. Higher %IncMSE values suggest that the variable is crucial for accurate prediction, while lower or negative values indicate limited or no contribution to the model’s predictive ability.
These importance scores allow us to rank the predictors, offering insights into which factors most strongly influence stop-and-search counts. The importance measures are central to our objectives, as they reveal key drivers of disparities and patterns in stop-and-search practices across different groups.




4.7.3 Interpretation of Random Forest Output
In the results, we focus on the variable importance scores to identify the most influential factors contributing to stop-and-search activity. This approach allows us to highlight demographic, regional, and contextual factors that may not show straightforward relationships but still play a significant role in total search volume. The random forest findings are interpreted in conjunction with the main regression model results to provide a comprehensive analysis of stop-and-search practices, validating key factors and uncovering complex relationships that inform policy recommendations.
By incorporating the random forest model into the analysis, we achieve a richer, multi-faceted understanding of stop-and-search dynamics, capturing both straightforward and complex patterns that contribute to observed disparities. This dual-model approach thus enhances the robustness and depth of the study’s findings, aligning with the project’s objective of identifying and addressing factors contributing to inequality in policing practices.

5.3 Modelling
This section outlines the statistical modelling approach applied to analyze stop and search data. Multiple models were constructed and evaluated, each targeting specific aspects of the data while considering methodological rigor. The focus was on understanding disparities across financial years, regions, and ethnic groups, controlling for key covariates such as sex, age group, and reason for search.

5.3.1 Overview of Models Tested

Model 1: Simple Linear Regression

A baseline linear regression model was fitted with the stop-and-search rate (rate) as the dependent variable.
Independent variables included financial year, region, ethnicity, sex, age group, and reason for search.
Diagnostics revealed significant heteroscedasticity, making this model unsuitable.

Model 2: Log-Transformed Linear Regression

To address heteroscedasticity, a logarithmic transformation of the rate (log(rate)) was applied.
The transformed model demonstrated improved fit and approximate normality in residuals.

Mixed Linear Model

A mixed-effects model was considered, treating financial year as a random effect to account for potential year-specific variability.
However, the random effect’s variance was close to zero, indicating that this added complexity was unnecessary.

Generalized Linear Model (GLM) with Offset

A Poisson GLM with a log link function was employed, using the number of searches as the dependent variable and the log population as an offset.
This model was particularly relevant for adjusting for population size across regions and demographics.
All parameters were highly significant (p < 0.0001), and the effect sizes for ethnic groups were consistent with findings from prior research.

Model Evaluation

Pseudo-R² by Cohen was used to assess the GLM’s fit. The pseudo-R² value confirmed the model’s adequacy for explaining variability in the data.




5.3.2 Key Considerations

Model Selection: While multiple models were tested, the GLM with an offset was identified as the most appropriate for the dataset, balancing interpretability and statistical validity.
Diagnostics: Each model was assessed for assumptions such as normality of residuals, heteroscedasticity, and random effects variance to ensure robustness.
Significance of Covariates: Across models, ethnicity consistently emerged as a significant factor, supporting the focus on disparities in stop-and-search practices.

These models provide a robust framework for understanding patterns and disparities in stop-and-search data, and they form the foundation for further statistical and interpretive analysis.
Based on the results of the evaluated models, a Poisson regression with a population offset was selected as the final model. The following section delves into the rationale, structure, and key findings of the chosen model.

5.4.2.3 Key Findings
The results show significant disparities in stop-and-search likelihoods. For instance, individuals identifying as Black or Black British are 3.02 times more likely to be stopped and searched compared to White individuals, with a 95% confidence interval of (2.85, 3.2). Similarly, males are 8 times more likely to be stopped and searched than females, highlighting a significant gender disparity.
London stands out with the highest regional rate: individuals there are 4.09 times as likely to be stopped and searched as those in the East Midlands (95% CI: 3.7–4.54).
These findings underscore critical disparities in stop-and-search practices across demographic and geographic dimensions.



5.4.3 Model Coefficients: Interpretation
This analysis evaluates the association between demographic, temporal, and geographic factors and police stop-and-search frequencies in England and Wales using a Poisson regression model. The model includes an offset for population size to account for differences in regional populations, providing rate ratios for stop-and-search frequencies across groups.
Key variables were encoded for interpretability: age group was binary, with “Under 25” for individuals aged 10–24 and “25 and over” for those 25 and above; reason for search was binary, with “Drugs” for drug-related stops and “Non-drugs” for other reasons. Baseline levels for categorical variables include: financial year 2020/21, region East Midlands, ethnicity White, sex Female, age group 25 and above, and reason for search non-drug-related. All coefficients are exponentiated to represent rate ratios.
Each rate ratio indicates the multiplicative effect of a variable on the likelihood of stop and search, relative to the baseline. Values greater than 1 represent increased likelihood, while values below 1 signify decreased likelihood.

5.4.3.1 Coefficients and Interpretations

5.4.3.1.1 Financial Year

2021/22: The rate ratio for 2021/22 is 0.73 (95% CI: 0.69–0.77), indicating that stop-and-search frequencies were approximately 0.73 times as likely compared to 2020/21.
2022/23: The rate ratio for 2022/23 is 0.74 (95% CI: 0.7–0.78).

These results suggest a consistent decrease in stop-and-search activities over time.


5.4.3.1.2 Region (Relative to East Midlands)
Most regions show higher stop-and-search rates than East Midlands, with London standing out. For instance: - London: Rate ratio of 4.09 (95% CI: 3.7–4.54). - South East: Rate ratio of 1.44 (95% CI: 1.28–1.61).
The variation across regions likely reflects differences in policing practices, crime profiles, and population density.


5.4.3.1.3 Ethnicity (Relative to White)
Ethnic minorities showed significantly different rates of stop and search compared to White individuals: - Black or Black British: Rate ratio of 3.02 (95% CI: 2.85–3.2), indicating a 202.2% higher likelihood of being stopped and searched.


5.4.3.1.4 Sex (Relative to Female)

Male: Rate ratio of 8 (95% CI: 7.55–8.49). Men are significantly more likely to be stopped and searched compared to women.



5.4.3.1.5 Age Group (Relative to Age 25+)

Under 25: Rate ratio of 1.03 (95% CI: 0.99–1.06), reflecting a slightly increased likelihood for younger individuals.



5.4.3.1.6 Reason for Search (Relative to Non-Drug Related)

Drug-Related: Rate ratio of 1.77 (95% CI: 1.71–1.84), indicating a substantial increase in stop-and-search likelihood for drug-related reasons.





5.4.4 Model Fit and Diagnostics

Pseudo R-squared (Cohen’s): The pseudo R-squared value of 0.884 indicates that the model explains approximately 88.4% of the variability in stop and search counts, suggesting a strong fit. This high explanatory power supports the model’s validity in identifying and quantifying the associations between stop and search practices and demographic, geographic, and temporal factors.

The residual deviance (342,749.3 on 1950 degrees of freedom) indicates a good model fit, with some remaining variability potentially attributable to unobserved factors. The estimated dispersion parameter is 181.8, confirming severe overdispersion; standard errors are scaled accordingly by the Quasi-Poisson family (see Methodology). AIC is not defined for Quasi-Poisson models.

Interaction model (ethnicity × financial year): To account for part of this overdispersion and allow ethnic disparities to vary over time, we fitted an extended model including an ethnicity × financial_year interaction. The interaction model reduces the dispersion parameter from 181.8 to 174.9 and improves the pseudo R² from 88.4% to 88.8%. An F-test confirms the interaction terms are jointly significant (p < 0.001), indicating that ethnic disparities have shifted meaningfully across financial years. Despite this improvement, the remaining overdispersion (\(\hat{\phi} \approx\) 175) reflects heterogeneity at the force level and other unmodelled factors,common feature of aggregate policing data. The Quasi-Poisson framework ensures that all reported confidence intervals and significance tests remain conservative regardless.



5.4.5 Addressing the Project Questions


5.4.6 Addressing the Project Questions

Do Black People in Metropolitan Areas Experience More Drug Stop and Searches?
To address this question, we analyze the combined effects of ethnicity (Black or Black British), region (London as a proxy for metropolitan area), and reason for search (drug-related):

Ethnicity (Black or Black British): The rate ratio is 3.02 (95% CI: 2.85–3.2), indicating Black individuals are approximately 3.02 times more likely to be stopped and searched compared to White individuals.
Region (London): The rate ratio for London relative to East Midlands is 4.09 (95% CI: 3.7–4.54), confirming that London has far higher search rates than the baseline region.
Reason for Search (Drug-Related): The rate ratio is 1.77 (95% CI: 1.71–1.84), indicating drug-related searches are approximately 1.77 times more likely than non-drug-related searches.

Combined effect: The multiplicative rate effect for Black individuals in London during drug-related stops is approximately 21.95 times that for White individuals in the East Midlands for non-drug-related reasons, holding sex and age constant.
What is the Relationship Between Young People Under 25 and Drug Stops?
For this question, we examine the effects of age group (under 25) and reason for search (drug-related):

Age Group (Under 25): The rate ratio is 1.03 (95% CI: 0.99–1.06), indicating individuals under 25 are approximately 1.03 times more likely to be stopped and searched compared to individuals aged 25 and above.
Reason for Search (Drug-Related): The rate ratio is 1.77 (95% CI: 1.71–1.84), suggesting that drug-related searches are approximately 1.77 times more likely than non-drug-related searches.

Combined effect: The multiplicative rate effect for individuals under 25 in drug-related stops is approximately 1.82 times more likely than for older individuals for non-drug-related reasons.

This analysis addresses two primary questions regarding drug-related stop-and-search practices in metropolitan areas:

Do Black Males under 25 Years of Age in Metropolitan Areas Experience More Drug Stop-and-Searches?
How Does This Compare to Black Females, White Females, and White Males under 25 in Metropolitan Areas, Specifically When the Reason for Stop and Search is Drug-Related?

5.4.8 Policy Implications
The identified disparities necessitate targeted interventions to ensure equitable policing practices:

Policy Review and Reform:

Implement Equitable Policing Guidelines: Develop and enforce guidelines that minimize racial and gender biases in stop-and-search operations.
Data Transparency: Mandate comprehensive data collection and public reporting on stop-and-search encounters to monitor and address disparities.

Training and Awareness:

Bias Training: Enhance training programs for law enforcement to recognize and mitigate unconscious biases that contribute to disproportionate targeting of specific demographic groups.
Cultural Competency: Foster cultural competency among police officers to improve interactions with diverse communities.

Community Engagement:

Build Trust: Engage with communities, particularly among young Black males, to build trust and cooperation between law enforcement and the populations they serve.
Feedback Mechanisms: Establish channels for community members to provide feedback and report instances of discriminatory practices without fear of retaliation.


By addressing these areas, policymakers and law enforcement agencies can work towards more fair and just policing strategies, ensuring that stop-and-search practices do not disproportionately affect specific demographic groups and that all individuals are treated equitably under the law.

title: 5  Results
section: 5.5 Random Forest Model: Machine Learning Approach
text:
5.5 Random Forest Model: Machine Learning Approach

A random forest model was used to identify the most influential factors associated with total stop-and-search activity across financial years, regions, and demographic groups. This approach complements the regression analysis by revealing complex, non-linear relationships between predictors and total searches. The random forest was trained on demographic and contextual variables, including financial year, region, ethnicity, sex, age group, reason for search, and population size, to determine the relative importance of each factor in predicting the total number of stop-and-searches. The variable importance measures (based on %IncMSE) highlight key factors that influence stop-and-search volume and allow an in-depth exploration of the project’s objectives.

5.5.1 Variable Importance and Interpretation
The variable importance plot (Figure X) shows each predictor’s contribution to the model, measured by % Increase in Mean Squared Error (%IncMSE). Key findings from the random forest analysis include:

Sex:

Sex emerged as the most influential predictor (%IncMSE = 61.8), the single strongest driver of search volume in the model. Consistent with the regression findings, males are disproportionately represented in stop-and-search activity. This alignment across model types underscores the persistent gender gap in policing.

Population:

Population size was the second most important predictor (%IncMSE = 36.8). Areas with larger populations experience higher total search counts, reflecting the concentration of searches in densely populated regions.

Region:

Region also displayed a high %IncMSE, suggesting that geographic location strongly influences stop-and-search activity. This regional variation likely reflects different policing strategies and priorities across England and Wales. The substantial impact of region on search volume suggests that certain areas are more intensely policed, which may be related to local crime rates, population density, or policy differences.

Ethnicity:

Ethnicity emerged as an influential factor, with notable %IncMSE values. Within the random forest model, Black or Black British individuals were particularly associated with higher search counts, reflecting the model’s capacity to capture ethnic disparities in policing. The importance of ethnicity aligns with the project’s focus on identifying demographic disparities in stop-and-search practices, confirming that specific ethnic groups are more frequently targeted in police searches.

Financial Year and Reason for Search:

Financial year and reason for search also contributed to the prediction of total searches, though to a lesser extent than population, sex, and region. The financial year variable’s influence suggests temporal changes in policing activity, potentially linked to policy adjustments or shifts in crime prevention focus over time. Drug-related stops (indicated by the reason for search variable) were also predictive of higher search counts, suggesting that specific search reasons contribute to variation in stop-and-search volume.

Age Group:

Age group exhibited a low and even negative %IncMSE, indicating that age group alone may not meaningfully enhance prediction accuracy in this model. This contrasts with the regression analysis, where age group had a positive association with search counts. The random forest results suggest that age might interact with other factors (like ethnicity or reason for search) rather than being a primary predictor of search volume independently.




5.5.2 Implications for Project Objectives
The random forest model findings align with the project’s objectives, providing detailed insights into factors influencing total stop-and-search counts and validating key areas of demographic disparity. The high importance of sex, population, and region reveals structural factors that drive search volumes across England and Wales, with clear implications for regional and demographic disparities in policing. The consistent influence of ethnicity across both the random forest and regression models underscores the model’s reliability in identifying areas where certain groups are disproportionately affected by stop-and-search practices.
In summary, the random forest analysis provides a robust exploration of the factors driving total stop-and-search volume. By identifying sex, population, region, and ethnicity as major predictors, the model highlights demographic and regional differences in policing practices. This evidence-based approach supports the project’s goal to uncover disparities and guide recommendations for more equitable policing policies across demographic groups.

title: 6  Discussion Section
text:
6.1 Interpretation of Results and Comparison with Government Findings
The analysis of stop and search practices reveals significant disparities across demographic groups and regions, providing insights that align closely with recent findings from the UK government’s 2023 report (Home Office (GOV.UK), 2023). Compared to baseline groups (e.g., White ethnicity, female gender, age 25 and older, and non-drug-related searches), certain groups, including Black individuals, young people under 25, and males, experience disproportionately higher stop and search rates. For example, our model, which accounts for variables such as age, region, and type of search, estimates that Black individuals are approximately 3 times more likely to be stopped than their White counterparts. This modelled rate contrasts with the government’s reported raw disparity rates, adjusted for population size only, of 4.1 to 5.5 for Black individuals compared to their White counterparts, offering a more nuanced understanding of the factors contributing to these disparities.
Beyond the modeled rates, we also compare raw disparity rates calculated directly from our data with those reported by the government. Although our findings align with the overall trends reported in Table 2.5 from the UK government’s report (Ibid.), the raw disparity rates are broadly consistent. For example, our analysis estimates that Asian individuals are 1.3 to 1.9 times more likely to be stopped than White individuals, which is consistent with the government’s reported disparity rate of 1.4 for 2022/23. Similarly, our analysis shows Black individuals are 3.6 to 5.5 times more likely to be stopped, consistent with the government’s reported range of 4.1 to 5.5. Minor differences stem from variations in population adjustments and processing methodologies, as our analysis uses raw census data for England and Wales, excluding BTP. Additionally, variations in how stop and search data are aggregated across financial years and regions may contribute to these differences. This includes how missing data are handled. In our case, we have removed missing data before the calculations. Despite methodological differences, both analyses highlight the persistent disproportionate impact.
The total number of stop and searches in our analysis closely aligns with the figures reported in the UK government’s 2023 report (Ibid.). For the year ending March 2023, our analysis estimates a total of 547,002 stop and searches, matching the government’s reported figure. Similarly, for the year ending March 2022, both our analysis and the government report a total of 530,970 searches. The trend of increasing stop and searches in recent years is consistent across both datasets, with a 3% increase observed from 2021/22 to 2022/23.
While the total counts align with government figures, the disparity rates highlight critical differences in how stop and searches are distributed across demographic groups. The random forest model, through variable importance measures, reinforces these findings by highlighting ethnicity and sex as key drivers of total search volume. This underscores a potential bias in stop and search deployment, particularly for drug-related stops where young individuals and ethnic minorities are overrepresented. Our results also show that stop and searches frequently lead to no further action (70% of cases), similar to findings in the government report, which notes that stop and search seldom culminates in arrests or legal outcomes.

title: 6  Discussion Section
section: 6.2 Contrasting with Vomfell and Stewart’s Findings on Officer Bias and Over-Patrolling
text:
6.2 Contrasting with Vomfell and Stewart’s Findings on Officer Bias and Over-Patrolling
Vomfell and Stewart’s study is a significant benchmark for understanding ethnic disparities in stop and search practices, particularly their focus on officer behavior and regional contexts. Our findings align with and extend the work of Vomfell and Stewart (2021) on ethnic disparities in stop and search. In their study, Vomfell and Stewart focus on “officer over-searching” and “over-patrolling” as contributors to the overrepresentation of minorities in stop and search practices. They find that officers search Black individuals 1.41 times more frequently than White individuals, even when controlling for local crime rates. Our analysis, however, reveals a broader pattern across regions and demographics, with Black individuals 3 times more likely to be stopped. This disparity may reflect systemic biases in both individual and institutional levels, extending beyond specific patrol areas to broader policy-driven practices.
The random forest model adds depth to these findings, capturing non-linear and interaction effects among variables such as region and ethnicity. The model identified population size as a significant driver of total searches, indicating that over-patrolling may be more concentrated in highly populated, ethnically diverse urban areas. This is consistent with Vomfell and Stewart’s findings on over-policing in metropolitan areas, such as London, which is disproportionately targeted for stop and search. Additionally, our models reveal that males are 8 times more likely than females to be subjected to stop and search, echoing Vomfell and Stewart’s observations that males aged 15-34 are concentrated in high-surveillance areas. Together, these insights suggest a feedback loop where over-policing in certain regions reinforces higher stop rates for ethnic minorities, potentially perpetuating biased policing practices.

title: 6  Discussion Section
text:
6.3 Implications for Policy and Policing
The integration of the regression and random forest models offers a more comprehensive view of disparities in stop and search practices, suggesting several policy implications. First, the high percentage of “no further action” cases indicates a need for more stringent criteria for initiating stops, especially in drug-related cases that disproportionately impact young individuals and ethnic minorities. The random forest’s emphasis on population and region as critical factors in predicting stop and search volume further suggests that over-patrolling in densely populated, ethnically diverse regions contributes to these disparities. Addressing this issue could involve adopting data-driven patrol strategies that minimize over-surveillance of specific demographic groups, as recommended by Vomfell and Stewart.
In conclusion, the combination of regression and random forest models offers robust insights into demographic and regional disparities in stop and search practices across England and Wales. The findings support a strong case for policy reform aimed at achieving more equitable policing practices, ensuring that stop and search policies do not disproportionately affect certain populations. Moving forward, further analysis could incorporate officer-level data to better assess individual contributions to these disparities, as Vomfell and Stewart suggest. This could enable policymakers to address both institutional and individual sources of bias within policing, ultimately supporting fairer and more effective law enforcement practices.

title: 6  Discussion Section
text:
6.4 Is the Disparity Getting Worse?
One of the most concerning findings of the extended five-year analysis is that the adjusted disparity for Black individuals has worsened over the period. The per-year Quasi-Poisson models reveal an adjusted Black/White IRR of 3 in 2020/21, falling briefly to 2.86 in 2021/22 before rising to 3.33 by 2024/25. This rising trend is statistically significant: the 2024/25 confidence interval (3–3.7) does not overlap with the 2021/22 estimate, indicating a genuine deterioration.
Crucially, this worsening occurs in the context of a substantial fall in absolute search volumes for Black individuals, from approximately 96,000 in 2020/21 to around 51,000 in 2024/25. The apparent paradox resolves when we note that White search volumes fell even faster over the same period, causing the relative disparity (after adjusting for population and other covariates) to widen. In other words, the reduction in stop and search activity since the 2020/21 peak has not been equally distributed across ethnic groups: Black communities have benefited proportionally less from the overall reduction.
The increase in the Mixed IRR, from 1.17 in 2020/21 to 1.7 in 2024/25, is also notable and merits closer attention in future analyses.

title: 6  Discussion Section
text:
6.5 The South West Anomaly
The regional analysis reveals that the South West has the highest Black/White unadjusted rate ratio (5.09×), significantly exceeding London (3.62×). This is counter-intuitive: London has a large, established Black community and has historically attracted the most scrutiny over stop and search. The South West, by contrast, has the smallest Black population of any English region (under 2%), which may contribute to a “visibility effect” in which Black individuals are more conspicuous to officers in predominantly White areas (Vomfell and Stewart, 2021).
This finding aligns with evidence that ethnic disproportionality is not simply an urban or metropolitan phenomenon. Forces such as Avon & Somerset and Devon & Cornwall operate in regions with very low Black population shares, yet produce some of the highest Black/White rate ratios in England. This suggests that national policy interventions focused exclusively on London and other major cities may miss a large share of the disproportionality problem.

title: 6  Discussion Section
section: 6.6 Outcome Disparity and Differential Suspicion Thresholds
text:
6.6 Outcome Disparity and Differential Suspicion Thresholds
The outcome analysis adds an important complementary perspective. Black individuals have the highest arrest rate (16.0%) of all ethnic groups, compared to 13.3% for White individuals, a gap of 2.7 percentage points. At first glance, this might suggest that searches of Black individuals are more productive, not less. However, this interpretation requires caution.
First, an arrest does not imply guilt; it is itself an exercise of discretionary police power. Second, given that Black individuals are stopped at over three times the adjusted rate of White individuals, even a slightly higher arrest-to-search conversion rate implies a vastly larger burden of unjustified stops for Black communities in absolute terms. The No Further Action rate of approximately 69% is broadly similar across ethnic groups, indicating that most searches, regardless of ethnicity, do not result in enforcement action.
The combination of a high search rate, similar NFA proportions, and a modestly higher arrest rate is consistent with a model in which officers apply a lower suspicion threshold to Black individuals before initiating a search: Black individuals are more frequently stopped, but when a stop does produce evidence, the outcome is broadly similar to other groups. This interpretation echoes the “hit rate” framework used in the literature to test for discriminatory targeting (Vomfell and Stewart, 2021).

title: 6  Discussion Section
section: 6.7 Disparity Is Not Explained by Search Reason
text:
6.7 Disparity Is Not Explained by Search Reason
A common counter-argument to claims of racial disproportionality is that it reflects enforcement focus rather than bias: if drug offending is concentrated in particular communities, higher drug-stop rates for Black individuals may reflect enforcement patterns rather than systemic targeting. The reason-by-reason analysis (see Section 5.10) tests this directly.
The results contradict the enforcement-focus hypothesis. The highest Black/White rate ratios are found not in drug stops (4.3×) but in anticipation of violence (7.9×), offensive weapons (6.9×), and terrorism searches (6.8×):non-drug categories with different legal powers, different officers, and different operational justifications. The disparity is even visible in negligible-volume categories such as drone searches (10.1×).
This is inconsistent with a drug-enforcement explanation. If that were driving the disparity, we would expect drug stops to show the highest ratio and other categories to approach parity. The opposite is observed. Instead, the data suggests that the lower suspicion threshold identified in the regression analysis operates across the full range of stop-and-search powers, not merely in drug contexts,consistent with a systemic rather than enforcement-specific pattern.

title: 6  Discussion Section
text:
6.8 Missing Ethnicity Data: Analytical Implications
The missing ethnicity analysis (see Section 5.11) raises important data quality considerations. Twenty-one forces have maintained more than 25% missing self-defined ethnicity consistently across the full five-year period. City of London Police averages 41.6% missing; Nottinghamshire 33.5%; Avon & Somerset 32%; Greater Manchester 28.6%.
As the Home Office notes, self-defined ethnicity is voluntary:individuals are not required to state their ethnicity during a stop and search ((GOV.UK), 2024). High missing rates may therefore reflect individuals declining to provide this information, differences in how officers ask, recording system transitions, or some combination of these. The data alone cannot distinguish between these explanations.
The analytical consequence is the same regardless of cause: searches without an ethnicity record are excluded from disparity calculations, meaning disparity estimates for high-missingness forces are based on incomplete data and should be interpreted cautiously. The missing data pattern is a limitation on the force-level conclusions of this analysis, not a finding in itself.
Notably, Avon & Somerset, the force serving the South West, which shows the highest regional Black/White ratio,as 32% mean missing ethnicity. This raises a question about whether the South West anomaly identified in section Section 6.5 is partly an artefact of which searches have ethnicity recorded, rather than solely a reflection of search rates.

title: 6  Discussion Section
section: 6.9 Limitations: Missing Data and Census Denominator Lag
text:
6.9 Limitations: Missing Data and Census Denominator Lag
Three limitations merit particular emphasis in interpreting these results.
Missing data on officer-defined ethnicity. A substantial share of records in the 5-year dataset are missing officer-defined ethnicity. This variable is important for distinguishing between self-identification (used in our models) and officer perception (the operationally relevant variable for a discrimination test). The self-defined ethnicity missing rate analysis (see Section 5.11 and Section 6.8) now documents which forces are responsible, but the officer-defined gap remains unresolved.
Census denominator lag. Population denominators are fixed at the 2021 Census, meaning that demographic changes, including migration, gentrification, and shifts in where ethnic minority populations reside, accumulate silently over the five-year period. By 2024/25, the 2021 figures may understate population growth in some areas and overstate it in others, potentially biasing the per-100,000 rates in unknown directions.
Force-level heterogeneity. The region-level analysis masks substantial variation among the 43 territorial forces within each region. Data on missing rates and search volumes by individual force (available in analysis/output/missing_by_force.csv and missing_persistent_forces.csv) show considerable heterogeneity. Aggregating to regions masks forces with especially high or low disparity, limiting the precision of the policy recommendations.

title: 7  Conclusion
text:
7.1 Key Findings
The five-year analysis (2020/21–2024/25) produces six headline findings:
These findings affirm UNJUST’s concerns about the disproportionate targeting of ethnic minorities and young people. The random forest model reinforced these results, explaining % of variance in search volumes andd identifying sex, population size, region, and ethnicity as the dominant predictors, and confirming non-linear interaction effects that compound disadvantage for specific demographic groups.
The disparities identified in stop-and-search practices, particularly among ethnic minorities and younger populations, emphasize the need to re-evaluate current policies to prevent over-policing and promote fairness within the criminal justice system. These insights align with recommendations from researchers such as Vomfell and Stewart (2021), who highlight the importance of addressing both over-patrolling of diverse areas and officer biases that disproportionately impact ethnic minorities. Together, these insights provide a robust foundation for advocating equitable policing practices.

title: 7  Conclusion
text:
Persistent and growing adjusted disparity: After controlling for region, sex, age, and reason for search, Black individuals face an adjusted incidence rate ratio of 3× in 2020/21, rising to 3.3× by 2024/25, a statistically significant worsening despite an overall fall in search volumes nationwide.
Intersection effects: Black males under 25 stopped for drug-related reasons in London face a combined stop rate approximately 21.9 times the rate of a White individual stopped for non-drug reasons in the East Midlands, holding sex and age constant.
Regional variation beyond London: The South West has the highest Black/White unadjusted ratio (5.1×), exceeding London (3.6×), demonstrating that ethnic disproportionality is a national problem rather than a metropolitan one.
Outcome disparity: Black individuals have one of the highest arrest rates following a search (16.0%, tied with Mixed) versus 13.3% for White individuals, yet similar No Further Action rates (~69%). This pattern is consistent with a lower suspicion threshold applied to Black individuals before initiating stops.
Racial skew spans every search reason: The Black/White rate gap is not confined to drug stops. The highest disparity is found in drone/unmanned aircraft searches (10.1×) and anticipation of violence (7.9×), followed by offensive weapons (6.9×) and terrorism searches (6.8×). Drug stops show a ratio of 4.3×. No major search reason approaches parity, indicating a systemic rather than enforcement-specific pattern (see Section 5.10).
Missing ethnicity data is concentrated in a subset of forces: Twenty-one forces average above 25% missing self-defined ethnicity across the five years. City of London Police averages 41.6% missing, Nottinghamshire 33.5%, and Avon & Somerset 32%. Because individuals are not required to disclose their ethnicity, the reasons for high missing rates cannot be determined from the data alone; the effect is that disparity estimates for these forces are based on incomplete records and should be interpreted with caution (see Section 5.11).

title: 7  Conclusion
text:
7.2 Evidence-Based Implications
The following observations arise directly from the statistical findings and are offered as evidence-based points for consideration. Questions about appropriate responses, including any policy or advocacy positions,re for UNJUST and relevant bodies to determine. The statistician’s role is to present what the data shows and to note where the findings raise questions that may be worth pursuing further.

Adjusted Disparity Trends Are Not Reflected in Current Official Reporting Published statistics on stop and search focus primarily on raw counts and unadjusted rate ratios. This analysis shows that the adjusted Black/White disparity, after accounting for region, sex, age, and reason for search,ose from 3× to 3.3× over five years, during a period in which overall search volumes fell. A worsening trend that is not visible in headline figures may warrant consideration by those responsible for the design of official statistical reporting.
Ethnic Disproportionality Extends Beyond Metropolitan Areas The South West records the highest Black/White unadjusted rate ratio (5.1×) of any region in England and Wales, substantially exceeding London (3.6×). This is consistent with a “visibility effect” in predominantly White regions, as discussed in the academic literature (Vomfell and Stewart, 2021). Analyses and oversight that focus exclusively on metropolitan forces may not capture the full national picture.
The No Further Action Rate Raises Questions About Consistency of Suspicion Thresholds Approximately 69% of all stops result in no further action across all ethnic groups. Combined with the higher stop rate for Black individuals and a modestly higher arrest rate (16.0% vs 13.3% for White individuals), this pattern is statistically consistent with a lower suspicion threshold being applied before initiating searches of Black individuals. The data identifies a pattern; the causes and appropriate responses are beyond the scope of this analysis.
Drug-Related Searches and the Intersection of Ethnicity, Age, and Sex The interaction analysis indicates that Black males under 25 stopped for drug-related reasons in London face a combined adjusted rate approximately 21.9 times higher than comparable White males. Given the high NFA rate for drug-related stops overall, the data raises questions about the consistency with which suspicion criteria are applied across demographic groups in this context.
Racial Disproportionality Is Not Explained by Search Reason One might expect drug enforcement, disproportionately targeted at Black individuals,o account for much of the overall disparity. The reason-by-reason analysis (see Section 5.10) shows this is not the case. Disparity is highest in low-volume, non-drug categories such as anticipation of violence (7.9×) and offensive weapons (6.9×). The gap in drug stops (4.3×) is in fact lower than for most other categories, suggesting that the hypothesis of drug-enforcement bias alone does not account for the overall pattern.
Missing Ethnicity Data Is Concentrated and Limits Force-Level Analysis The missing ethnicity analysis (see Section 5.11) identifies a group of forces, including City of London, Nottinghamshire, and Greater Manchester,hat have maintained high missing rates (29–42%) consistently over the full five-year period. Self-defined ethnicity is voluntary under Home Office guidance, so high missing rates may reflect individuals declining to disclose, differences in recording practice, or system transitions; ;ese cannot be separated from the data. The consequence is that disparity estimates for high-missingness forces are based on a partial record of their stops, and force-level comparisons should be treated with corresponding caution.
Census Denominator Lag Introduces Uncertainty in Rate Calculations All per-100,000 rates rely on 2021 Census denominators. By 2024/25, demographic changes, particularly population growth and redistribution in urban areas,ill have accumulated over four years. The direction and scale of any resulting bias in disparity rates is unknown. Whether more timely population estimates could improve the accuracy of future analyses is a question the data highlights but cannot itself resolve.

title: 7  Conclusion
text:
7.3 Closing Statement
This project equips UNJUST with valuable insights into the complexities of stop-and-search practices, emphasizing both their role in maintaining public safety and the disparities that warrant careful consideration. By shedding light on these nuances and identifying areas for improvement, UNJUST can contribute constructively to discussions with policymakers, law enforcement, and communities. These efforts aim to support ongoing progress toward a policing approach that balances public safety with fairness and equity.
